name: The Millennium Prize Problems
statement: Seven great open problems, each worth a million dollars, chosen for the year 2000.
meaning: The Millennium Prize Problems are seven unsolved problems in mathematics selected and announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute on 24 May 2000, at a meeting in Paris at the College de France, each carrying a prize of one million United States dollars for the first correct solution. They were chosen to highlight some of the most important and difficult open problems in mathematics at the turn of the millennium, in conscious homage to David Hilbert's list of 23 problems from 1900. The seven problems are the P versus NP problem, in computer science; the Hodge conjecture, in algebraic geometry; the Poincare conjecture, in topology; the Riemann hypothesis, in number theory; the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem, in mathematical physics; the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, in the theory of partial differential equations; and the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, in number theory. As of today, six remain unsolved; only the Poincare conjecture has been solved, by Grigori Perelman, whose proof appeared in 2002 and 2003 and who was awarded the prize in 2010 but declined it, along with the Fields Medal offered in 2006. The Riemann hypothesis is notable for appearing on both Hilbert's list, as part of his eighth problem, and the Millennium list, the only problem common to both. The problems were announced by John Tate and Michael Atiyah.
mechanism: The Millennium Prize Problems function as a curated set of grand challenges intended to focus and inspire mathematical research, backed by prestige and a substantial monetary prize. The Clay Mathematics Institute, a private foundation, assembled a committee of leading mathematicians to select problems that were widely recognized as central, deep, and long-standing, so that solving any one would represent a major advance, and it attached to each a one-million-dollar prize and a formal set of rules governing how a solution is to be verified and awarded, typically requiring publication and a period of scrutiny by the community. The choice deliberately echoed Hilbert's celebrated 1900 address, which had shaped a century of mathematics, and the year-2000 timing and Paris setting made the homage explicit. The seven problems span the breadth of modern mathematics and its applications, from the foundations of computation in P versus NP, through the deep number theory of the Riemann hypothesis and the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, the algebraic geometry of the Hodge conjecture, and the topology of the Poincare conjecture, to the mathematical physics of Yang-Mills theory and the analysis of the Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow. The single solved problem, the Poincare conjecture, illustrates the process and its surprises: Perelman solved it using Ricci flow, his proof was verified over several years, and he then declined both the Clay prize and the Fields Medal, a rare refusal that drew wide attention. The remaining six continue to stand as beacons for the field.

whyItMatters: The Millennium Prize Problems are the most famous set of open problems in contemporary mathematics, and they have played a significant role in shaping public awareness of the field and in focusing research attention on some of its deepest questions. By selecting, at the turn of the millennium, seven problems judged among the most important and difficult, and backing each with a one-million-dollar prize, the Clay Mathematics Institute created a modern counterpart to Hilbert's century-defining 1900 list, giving mathematicians and the public alike a shared sense of the great outstanding challenges. The problems span the breadth of mathematics and its connections to computer science and physics, so that progress on any one would resonate widely. The list has also generated compelling human drama, above all the solution of the Poincare conjecture by Grigori Perelman and his subsequent refusal of both the prize money and the Fields Medal, which brought mathematics rare popular attention and provoked reflection on recognition, motivation, and the culture of the discipline.

limits: The Millennium Prize Problems are a curated list rather than a comprehensive or canonical one, and several caveats apply. The selection reflects the judgment of the Clay committee at the year 2000 and does not claim to be the only or the definitive set of great problems; other important open questions were not included, and the choices, while widely respected, are not beyond discussion. Only one of the seven has been solved, and after more than two decades the remaining six, some of them extraordinarily hard, show no sign of imminent resolution, so the list is more a statement of aspiration than a schedule of expected progress. The single solved case, the Poincare conjecture, followed an unusual course, with Perelman's proof requiring years of community verification and his declining of the prize complicating the award process. Some historical details reward care: the announcement was made on 24 May 2000 in Paris, the problems were announced by John Tate and Michael Atiyah, and the description of the event as an homage to, rather than a reversal of, Hilbert's 1900 address is the accurate framing.
misreadings: The Millennium Prize Problems are not a complete list of the hardest problems in mathematics, but a selection made by the Clay Institute in 2000. They are not mostly solved; six of the seven remain open, with only the Poincare conjecture resolved. And the prize is not automatically paid on any claim, but only after verification under the Institute's rules, as Perelman's case showed, so treating the list as comprehensive, as largely solved, or as paying out on any announcement, misreads it.
